1.note: The author is using the name **Israel** to represent that man’s descendants. See the discussion of this usage in the introduction to this book. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And all of the Israelites were enrolled]

The expression **written** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and you can read their names]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And because of their transgression, Judah were exiled to Babylon]

The author is using the name **Judah** to represent the people of that kingdom. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the Judeans were exiled to Babylon]

The expression **were exiled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the Babylonians exiled the Judeans]

2.note: The author is using the name **Israel** to represent Israelites who were not priests or Levites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [were some Israelites]

The term **Nethinim** describes people who worked in the temple as servants of the priests and Levites. Many interpreters identify them with the descendants of the Gibeonites, based on Joshua 9:27. Alternate translation: [and temple servants]

3.q: וּ⁠בִ⁠ירוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ יָשְׁב֔וּ מִן־בְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה וּ⁠מִן־בְּנֵ֣י בִנְיָמִ֑ן וּ⁠מִן־בְּנֵ֥י אֶפְרַ֖יִם וּ⁠מְנַשֶּֽׁה
3.note: In each instance here and often in the rest of this chapter, the author is using the term **sons** to mean “descendants.” Alternate translation: [And descendants of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh dwelled in Jerusalem]

4.q: עוּתַ֨י בֶּן־עַמִּיה֤וּד בֶּן־עָמְרִי֙ בֶּן־אִמְרִ֣י בֶן־בני⁠מן־בְּנֵי־פֶ֖רֶץ בֶּן־יְהוּדָֽה
4.note: Since the next two verses put the name of a family’s clan within the tribe of Judah before the name of that family or its leader, you may wish to put the information in this verse in the same order. Alternate translation: [From the sons of Perez, the son of Judah: Uthai, the son of Ammihud, the son of Omri, the son of Imri, the son of Bani]

5.note: The word translated as **Shilonite** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense, since that word describes people from the city of Shiloh, which was in the territory of Ephriaim. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation, which says “Shelanite,” describing people from the clan of the tribe of Judah descended from his son Shelah. Numbers 26:20 supports that reading. If there is a major translation in your area, you may want to follow its reading. Alternate translation: [text]

The author is not referring to a specific **Shilonite** (or Shelanite). He means the Shilonites (or Shelanites) in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Shilonites] or [the Shelanites]

9.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 5:7. Alternate translation: [as their genealogies record them]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The phrase **heads of fathers** is short for “heads of fathers’ houses” or “heads of houses of fathers.” You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [All of these men were heads of houses of fathers]

9.q: כָּל־אֵ֣לֶּה אֲנָשִׁ֔ים רָאשֵׁ֥י אָב֖וֹת לְ⁠בֵ֥ית אֲבֹתֵי⁠הֶֽם
9.note: Since **fathers** means **houses of fathers**, it might seem that this full statement contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [All of these men were leaders in the house of their fathers] or [All of these men were clan leaders]

11.note: You may wish to make clear that this phrase applies to **Azariah** rather than to **Ahitub**. Alternate translation: [the son of Ahitub. Azariah was the leader of the house of God]
To translate this expression here and in verse 13, see how you translated the similar expression in 6:32. Alternate translation: [the temple of God]

13.note: The author is speaking as if the other priests who returned from exile were the actual **brothers** of the five priests he names with their lineages. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and their fellow priests]

The author is speaking as if these priests were actually **warriors** who fought with **valor**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [very capable men]

16.note: The author is not referring to a specific **Netophathite**. He means the members of that clan in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Netophathites]

17.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 9:13. Alternate translation: [and their fellow gatekeepers]

18.q: וְֽ⁠עַד־הֵ֔נָּה בְּ⁠שַׁ֥עַר הַ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ מִזְרָ֑חָ⁠ה הֵ֚מָּה הַ⁠שֹּׁ֣עֲרִ֔ים
18.note: Be sure that it is clear in your translation that the phrase **until now** refers to the time when the author wrote 1 Chronicles centuries ago. Avoid giving the impression that the expression refers to the present day of your own readers. Alternate translation: [And after they returned from exile, at the Gate of the King from the east, they were gatekeepers]

The author is describing the location of one place relative to another in the way that is characteristic of his culture. He means that if someone entered the temple courtyard through this **gate**, he would be coming **from the east**. In your translation, express this in the way your culture describes the relative location of places. Alternate translation: [to the east] or [on the east side of the courtyard]

As in 6:32, the author is using a situation from earlier in the Israelites’ history to represent a later situation in order to depict the continuity of their worship of Yahweh down through the generations. He is referring to the way the Levites camped all around the tabernacle as the Israelites traveled through the wilderness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from among the ranks of the Levites] or [from among the members of the tribe of Levi]

19.note: While the term **son** appears to be literal in its first instance, in the next two instances it means “descendant.” Alternate translation: [And Shallum, the son of Kore, a descendant of Ebiasaph, a descendant of Korah]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:13. Alternate translation: [and his fellow Levites]

**Ebiasaph** is the same person whom the author calls Asaph in [26:1](ta:26). Recall whether your translation team decided to use the same name for a given person in each place where he appears or whether you decided to use the name that the biblical author does, even if that is a variant. Alternate translation: [Asaph]

The author is once again using a situation from earlier in the Israelites’ history to represent a later situation in order to depict the continuity of their worship of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [the temple]
The author is using the word translated as **and** to introduce a comparison. Alternate translation: [just as their fathers]
The author is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [just as their ancestors]
The author is speaking of the sacred tent as if it had been a **camp** in which Yahweh lived in the wilderness. Alternate translation: [had been responsible for the tabernacle]

20.note: The author is using **to their faces** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in their presence.” He means that Phinehas had personally supervised the Levite gatekeepers. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [supervised them personally as their leader]

The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that Yahweh helped Phinehas. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh helped him]

21.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 9:19. Alternate translation: [to the temple]

22.q: כֻּלָּ֤⁠ם הַ⁠בְּרוּרִים֙ לְ⁠שֹׁעֲרִ֣ים בַּ⁠סִּפִּ֔ים מָאתַ֖יִם וּ⁠שְׁנֵ֣ים עָשָׂ֑ר
22.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that there were **212** of these gatekeepers with the information that this was **All of them**. Alternate translation: [All 212 of them were chosen as gatekeepers at the thresholds]

The author does not mean that these 212 gatekeepers **were chosen** for that duty after they returned from exile. He means that they belonged to the clans that David and Samuel had chosen to do this work. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [All of them belonged to the clans that had been chosen as gatekeepers]

The expression **were chosen** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [All of them belonged to the clans whose responsibility it was to keep the gates]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:7. Alternate translation: [Their genealogies recorded in what villages their clans lived]

22.q: הֵ֣מָּה יִסַּ֥ד דָּוִ֛יד וּ⁠שְׁמוּאֵ֥ל הָ⁠רֹאֶ֖ה בֶּ⁠אֱמוּנָתָֽ⁠ם
22.note: The author is saying **They** at the start of the sentence to emphasize that these Levites had a legitimate role as gatekeepers. It may be more natural in your language to put this reference to them later in the sentence. Alternate translation: [David and Samuel the seer established them in their trust]

Here, **trust** represents an “office” or “responsibility” that a person in authority would entrust to someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in their office]

23.note: The author is speaking as if these Levites who returned from exile were the actual **sons** of the Levites whom David and Samuel originally appointed. He means that they were his descendants. Alternate translation: [and later their descendants]

The author is using the term **house** in the first instance to mean the temple, in which Yahweh was present in a special way, as if it were a house in which he lived. But the author is mindful that during the time of David, the sacred chest was in a special tent that David had set up for it. It was David’s son Solomon who later built the temple. So in the second instance, the term **house** identifies this **tent** as Yahweh’s dwelling at the time. Alternate translation: [of Yahweh’s sanctuary, which was a tent at the time]

24.note: The author is using **winds** as a common expression of his culture to mean “directions.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in four quarters] or [on the four sides of the temple courtyard]

The author is stating these directions in the order that was customary in his culture. It may be more natural for you to put them in the order that is customary in your culture. Alternate translation: [north, east, south, and west]

25.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 9:17. Alternate translation: [And their fellow gatekeepers]

The pronoun **these** refers to “the four chiefs of the gatekeepers” who are described in the next verse and who are named in verse 17. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to work with the chief gatekeepers]

26.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but some important information. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Now]

26.q: בֶ⁠אֱמוּנָ֞ה הֵ֗מָּה אַרְבַּ֨עַת֙ גִּבֹּרֵ֣י הַ⁠שֹּׁעֲרִ֔ים הֵ֖ם הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֑ם
26.note: The author is once again stressing the continuity of the community’s worship arrangements. He is making clear that the men in this important role at the temple were **Levites**, not men without that lineage whom the governor may have appointed. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these four men who served in the important office of chiefs of the gatekeepers were Levites]

26.q: הֵ֗מָּה אַרְבַּ֨עַת֙ גִּבֹּרֵ֣י הַ⁠שֹּׁעֲרִ֔ים הֵ֖ם הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֑ם
26.note: The author says **they** twice to emphasize that these **chiefs of the gatekeepers** had the necessary lineage as **Levites**. It might seem that repeating these pronouns would be to express extra information that would not be natural in your language. If so, you can convey the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [the four chiefs of the gatekeepers were genuine Levites]
To translate this expression here and in the next verse, see how you translated the similar expression in 9:11. Alternate translation: [the temple of God]

27.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And because the watch was upon them, they lodged around the house of God]

The author is speaking as if the **watch** (that is, the duty of watching or guarding the temple area) had actually been **upon** or on top of these men. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it was their responsibility to guard the temple area]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **the opening**, he means the opening of the gates to the temple courtyard. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [responsible for opening the courtyard gates]

The author is using this common expression of his culture to mean “every morning.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [morning after morning] or [every morning]

28.note: Here and in the next verse, the pronoun **them** refers to the gatekeepers. Alternate translation: [And some of the gatekeepers]

Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. The explanation is implied, not stated, but you could state it in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the service. To ensure that none were lost,]

The author is saying **in** to mean “in to the temple courtyard,” and he is saying **out** to mean “out of the courtyard and back to the temple storerooms.” It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [by number they brought them in to the temple courtyard, and by number they brought them back out to the temple storerooms]

29.note: The expression **were born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in another way that would be natural in your language. (Since the agent is unclear, it would be preferable not to use an active form and suggest an agent.) Alternate translation: [And some of them were responsible for]

30.note: The author is using the phrase **sons of** to indicate that these people had the characteristic of something. In this case, he means that these people had the characteristic of being **priests**. Alternate translation: [And some of the priests]

32.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 6:33. Alternate translation: [And some from the clan of the Kohathites]

See how you translated the similar expression in 9:13. The author means that the Kohathites were fellow Levites with the Korahites, whom he has been describing in verses 19–31. Alternate translation: [from their fellow Levites]

The author is using this common expression of his culture to mean “for every Sabbath.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Sabbath by Sabbath] or [for every Sabbath]

33.q: וְ⁠אֵ֣לֶּה הַ֠⁠מְשֹׁרְרִים רָאשֵׁ֨י אָב֧וֹת לַ⁠לְוִיִּ֛ם בַּ⁠לְּשָׁכֹ֖ת פטירים כִּֽי־יוֹמָ֥ם וָ⁠לַ֛יְלָה עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֖ם בַּ⁠מְּלָאכָֽה
33.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And because these, the singers, heads of fathers of the Levites in the chambers, were over them day and by night in the work, they were free]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **the chambers**, he means the chambers or rooms that adjoined the temple. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [who stayed in the temple chambers]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **free**, he means “free from any other obligations.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [were free from any other obligations]

The author is using the two main components of time, day and night, to mean all of time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [constantly]

The pronoun **them** refers to the Levite singers whom these **heads of fathers** (clan leaders) supervised. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these leaders supervised the other Levite singers]

34.q: אֵלֶּה֩ רָאשֵׁ֨י הָ⁠אָב֧וֹת לַ⁠לְוִיִּ֛ם לְ⁠תֹלְדוֹתָ֖⁠ם רָאשִׁ֑ים
34.note: The author is using the term **heads** to mean “leaders” in two different senses in this verse. Alternate translation: [These men who were Levite clan leaders according to their generations were supervisors]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:7. Alternate translation: [as listed in their genealogies]

35.note: The pronoun **they** does not refer to the Levites whom the author has been discussing. Instead, it refers to some members of the tribe of Benjamin. As the introduction to this chapter discusses, from here to the end of the chapter, the author is repeating the genealogy of Saul from 8:29–38 in order to introduce his history of the Israelite kings. So that your readers can appreciate what the author is doing, translate this passage the way you translated the earlier one, allowing for minor differences in detail. Alternate translation: [Some Benjaminites dwelled in Gibeon]

37.note: Note that in this passage, the name **Mikloth** occurs at the end of this verse and at the beginning of the next verse. In the parallel in 8:31–32, the name occurs only once.

38.note: The name **Shimeam** is an older form of the name “Shimeah,” which occurs in the parallel in 8:32. If you have decided to use the same name for the same person throughout your translation, you may wish to use that name here. Alternate translation: [and Shimeah]

41.note: The name **Tahrea** is an older form of the name “Tarea,” which occurs in the parallel in 8:35. If you have decided to use the same name for the same person throughout your translation, you may wish to use that name here. Alternate translation: [and Tarea]

Some ancient versions add “and Ahaz,” as in the parallel in 8:35. It seems likely that this was the original reading, and you may wish to follow it in your translation. Alternate translation: [and Tahrea and Ahaz] or [and Tarea and Ahaz]

42.note: the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today reads “Jarah.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “Jadah,” which is a shortened form of the name Jehoaddah, which occurs in the parallel in 8:36. If you have decided to use the same name for the same person throughout your translation, you may wish to use a form of that name here. Alternate translation: [Jadah. And Jadah] or [Jehoaddah. And Jehoaddah]

44.note: Note that in this passage, the author says **These**, while in the parallel in 8:38, he says “All of these.”
